title: Ultrametric organization of energy landscapes on random Erdős--Rényi graphs: topological origin of barrier hierarchy
abstract: We investigate the ultrametric organization of energy landscapes defined on sparse random Erdős--Rényi graphs. Each graph vertex is assigned a random free energy from a uniform distribution over an interval of width $ΔF$, and the kinetics are modeled by a Markov process with Kramers transition rates. Using spectral decomposition of the rate matrix, we construct a kinetic Mahalanobis metric between basins of attraction. Computational experiments for graphs with $V=5000$ vertices and $E=5000$ edges show that the degree of nontrivial ultrametricity increases monotonically from $\approx42\%$ for $ΔF=10$ kJ/mol to $\approx96\%$ for $ΔF=1000$ kJ/mol. We prove a limit theorem: as $ΔF\to\infty$, the logarithmic asymptotics of this metric converge pointwise to the classical single-linkage ultrametric. For finite $ΔF$, corrections from suboptimal paths are exponentially suppressed with increasing $ΔF$, so that the metric becomes asymptotically ultrametric. Our results suggest that ultrametricity is a universal property of sparse, locally tree-like networks with rugged energy landscapes in the limit of large energy spreads.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the energy landscapes on sparse random graphs to determine if they possess a universal ultrametric organization. By comparing a kinetically derived metric with the ideal single-linkage ultrametric, the authors prove that this hierarchy emerges robustly when the energy differences are large. This suggests that local tree-like topology dictates the long-term dynamical structure of such complex systems.
main_problem: The study investigates whether the energy landscape organization on sparse random graphs exhibits universal ultrametricity in the limit of large energy spreads.
main_result: The kinetic metric between basins converges pointwise to the classical single-linkage ultrametric as the energy spread ($\Delta F$) tends to infinity, suggesting ultrametricity is a universal property for such systems.
method: The authors use spectral decomposition on a transformed rate matrix (Mahalanobis metric) and prove limit theorems comparing this kinetic distance to the minimax/single-linkage distance.
model_or_system: The system models energy landscapes defined by random free energies ($F_i$) assigned to vertices of sparse Erdős–Rényi graphs. Dynamics are governed by a continuous-time Markov process described by transition rates derived from these free energies.
key_observables: Degree of nontrivial ultrametricity, kinetic Mahalanobis metric $D(B_a, B_b)$, and the single-linkage ultrametric $ho(0)(B_a, B_b)$.
important_parameters: Energy spread ($\Delta F$), Temperature ($T$), Graph connectivity (sparse/locally tree-like).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that for large $\Delta F$, the contribution from suboptimal paths is exponentially suppressed, allowing the kinetic metric to be dominated by the minimax path.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the Markovian dynamics and constructing a computable symmetric metric (Chunk 2), to establishing the mathematical link between this kinetic metric and the single-linkage ultrametric via limit theorems (Chunks 1 & 3), culminating in a discussion of topological origins (Chunk 4).
why_interesting: The concept of energy landscape organization into an ultrametric structure is highly relevant for understanding complex dynamics, relaxation pathways, and metastable states in disordered quantum systems or molecular folding processes.
